title: Second and third normal forms
description: A practical guide to separating partial and transitive dependencies in a hypothetical retail order dataset without losing the meaning of order headers, line items, products, and customers.
lead: Second and third normal forms solve different problems that often appear together in order data. Second normal form asks whether a non-key fact depends on only part of a composite key. Third normal form asks whether a non-key fact depends on another non-key fact. This article uses a small hypothetical retail order fixture to separate those two cases and show where each attribute belongs.

sections.heading: Start with the key, not with the table name
paragraphs: Assume a hypothetical retail dataset arrives as one wide relation named order_line_extract. Each row represents one purchased SKU on one order. The natural row identifier is the pair order_id and sku, because one order can contain several SKUs and one SKU can appear on many orders. For this example, assume a given SKU appears at most once per order; if the source permits duplicate lines for the same SKU, line_number would need to be part of the key instead.
The important candidate key is therefore order_id, sku. Every non-key attribute should be checked against that whole key before deciding whether the table is in second or third normal form.

Here is the hypothetical starting relation: order_line_extract(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_email, customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name, quantity, unit_price_at_order).

The relation is already shaped as rows, not repeating columns, so this guide does not cover first normal form. The problem here is dependency placement. Some facts describe the order, some describe the product, some describe the customer, some describe the category, and some describe the order line itself.
bullets: Candidate key for the starting relation: order_id, sku.
Line-level facts: quantity and unit_price_at_order depend on the order and the SKU together.
Order-level facts: order_date and customer_id depend on order_id alone.
Product-level facts: product_name and category_id depend on sku alone.
Customer and category descriptors introduce third-normal-form questions after second normal form has been addressed.

sections.heading: Second normal form: remove partial dependencies
paragraphs: Second normal form is about full dependence on a composite key. If a table has a single-column key, partial dependency is not the issue. If the key is composite, each non-key attribute must depend on the whole key, not on just one component of it.

In the hypothetical order_line_extract relation, order_date depends on order_id, not on the pair order_id, sku. Repeating order_date on every line of an order creates an update anomaly: correcting the date for order 1001 requires changing every line for that order. The same is true for customer_id. The value is chosen by the order header, not by each product line.

Product facts have the symmetric problem. product_name depends on sku alone. category_id also depends on sku alone in this example. Repeating product_name on every order line creates the possibility that SKU MUG-RED is called “Red mug” on one historical line and “Red ceramic mug” on another. That inconsistency is not an order-line fact; it is a misplaced product fact.

A second-normal-form decomposition separates the facts whose determinants are order_id and sku from the facts whose determinant is the whole composite key. At this stage, the tables can be orders(order_id, order_date, customer_id, customer_email, customer_tier), products(sku, product_name, category_id, category_name), and order_lines(order_id, sku, quantity, unit_price_at_order).

Notice one deliberate choice: unit_price_at_order stays on order_lines. A common counterexample is to move price to products because price seems product-related. But in an order dataset, the price charged for a SKU can vary by order because of promotions, contracts, markdowns, taxes, or historical price changes. In this example, unit_price_at_order is determined by the pair order_id, sku, not by sku alone. Moving it to products would overwrite history with a current product attribute.
bullets: Partial dependency: order_id determines order_date and customer_id even though the table key is order_id, sku.
Partial dependency: sku determines product_name and category_id even though the table key is order_id, sku.
Not a partial dependency in this example: order_id, sku determines quantity and unit_price_at_order.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL based on the hypothetical example.
-- It expresses the 2NF split; it is not evidence of execution.

CREATE TABLE orders_2nf (
  order_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date date NOT NULL,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL,
  customer_email text NOT NULL,
  customer_tier text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE products_2nf (
  sku text PRIMARY KEY,
  product_name text NOT NULL,
  category_id integer NOT NULL,
  category_name text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_lines_2nf (
  order_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES orders_2nf(order_id),
  sku text NOT NULL REFERENCES products_2nf(sku),
  quantity integer NOT NULL,
  unit_price_at_order numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);

sections.heading: Third normal form: remove transitive dependencies
paragraphs: After the second-normal-form split, two tables still carry a different kind of problem. The orders_2nf table has customer_email and customer_tier. Those attributes are not partial dependencies because orders_2nf has a single-column key, order_id. But they are still not facts about the order if customer_id determines them.

The dependency chain is order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines customer_email and customer_tier. That means order_id determines customer_email through another non-key attribute. This is a transitive dependency.

The products_2nf table has the same pattern if category_id determines category_name. The chain is sku determines category_id, and category_id determines category_name. category_name is therefore transitively dependent on sku through category_id.

Third normal form removes those transitive dependencies by creating referenced tables for the intermediate determinants. The revised design is orders(order_id, order_date, customer_id), customers(customer_id, customer_email, customer_tier), products(sku, product_name, category_id), categories(category_id, category_name), and order_lines(order_id, sku, quantity, unit_price_at_order).

This does not mean every descriptive text must be split into its own table. The split is justified by a dependency claim. If customer_tier is assigned per customer, then customer_tier belongs with customers. If a tier is recalculated per order at purchase time and intentionally frozen, then it may belong with orders under a different name, such as customer_tier_at_order. Normalization follows the business meaning of the fact, not the English noun in the column name.
bullets: Transitive dependency in orders_2nf: order_id determines customer_id, and customer_id determines customer_email and customer_tier.
Transitive dependency in products_2nf: sku determines category_id, and category_id determines category_name.
Third normal form keeps non-key attributes dependent on keys, not on other non-key attributes.

sections.heading: Counterexamples that separate the two normal forms
paragraphs: The distinction becomes clearer when the same attribute is tested in two different places.

Counterexample 1: customer_email in the original order_line_extract table violates more than one idea, but the first thing to notice is the partial dependency through order_id. Because order_id determines customer_id for the whole order, and the customer values repeat on every line, the wide table is not in second normal form. After customer information is moved out of order_lines and order headers, the remaining question is third normal form: does customer_id determine customer_email? If yes, customer_email belongs in customers.

Counterexample 2: category_name in the original table may look like a product detail, but the determinant matters. If sku determines category_id and category_id determines category_name, then category_name is not directly a SKU fact. In a 2NF-only design, products_2nf still repeats category_name for every product in the same category. Renaming “Drinkware” to “Kitchen drinkware” would require updating many product rows. Third normal form puts the name in categories.

Counterexample 3: unit_price_at_order should not be normalized away merely because a product table exists. Suppose order 1001 sold SKU MUG-RED for 12.00 and order 1002 sold the same SKU for 10.00 during a promotion. Those two rows do not contradict the dependency order_id, sku determines unit_price_at_order. They contradict the incorrect dependency sku determines unit_price_at_order. The correct design keeps the charged price on the line item.

Counterexample 4: product_name may be a product fact in this simplified model, but some retail systems store product_name_at_order to preserve the label shown to the customer at checkout. That would be a different attribute with different semantics. product_name belongs to products only if the model intends the current product name. product_name_at_order belongs to order_lines or another order snapshot structure if the model intends historical display text.

sections.heading: A diagnostic for proposed dependencies
paragraphs: A dataset cannot prove a functional dependency for all future data, but it can disprove one with a counterexample. The following illustrative query uses a small hypothetical fixture and looks for determinants that map to more than one dependent value.

The expected result for the first diagnostic is no rows for order_id determining order_date and customer_id in the sample. That supports, but does not prove, the modeling assumption that those are order-header facts. The expected result for the unit_price_at_order diagnostic is SKU MUG-RED, because the same SKU appears with two prices. That is useful evidence against placing unit_price_at_order in products.

Use this diagnostic as a modeling aid, not as a substitute for business rules. If the data contains bad historical records, a query may show violations of a rule that is still intended to be true. If the sample is too small, a query may miss violations that appear later. The durable decision comes from both observed data and the declared meaning of the attributes.
bullets: Ask: what is the determinant?
Check whether the determinant is the whole key, part of the key, or another non-key attribute.
Treat query results as counterexample search, not mathematical proof.
Name historical snapshot attributes explicitly when they differ from current master data attributes.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative dependency diagnostic using a hypothetical retail fixture.
-- These queries are intended to show the reasoning pattern.

WITH order_line_extract(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_email,
                        customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name,
                        quantity, unit_price_at_order) AS (
  VALUES
    (1001, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test',  'gold',   'Red mug',  20, 'Drinkware', 2, 12.00),
    (1001, 'TEA-BLK',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test',  'gold',   'Black tea', 30, 'Tea',       1,  8.50),
    (1002, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-06', 502, 'bo@example.test',   'silver', 'Red mug',  20, 'Drinkware', 1, 10.00),
    (1003, 'KETTLE-1', DATE '2026-01-07', 501, 'ana@example.test',  'gold',   'Kettle',   20, 'Drinkware', 1, 35.00)
)
SELECT order_id
FROM order_line_extract
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT order_date) > 1
    OR COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) > 1;

WITH order_line_extract(order_id, sku, order_date, customer_id, customer_email,
                        customer_tier, product_name, category_id, category_name,
                        quantity, unit_price_at_order) AS (
  VALUES
    (1001, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test',  'gold',   'Red mug',  20, 'Drinkware', 2, 12.00),
    (1001, 'TEA-BLK',  DATE '2026-01-05', 501, 'ana@example.test',  'gold',   'Black tea', 30, 'Tea',       1,  8.50),
    (1002, 'MUG-RED',  DATE '2026-01-06', 502, 'bo@example.test',   'silver', 'Red mug',  20, 'Drinkware', 1, 10.00),

)
SELECT sku, COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price_at_order) AS observed_price_count
FROM order_line_extract
GROUP BY sku
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price_at_order) > 1;

sections.heading: A compact decision rule
paragraphs: For a composite-key order-line table, second normal form is the first pass: remove attributes that depend only on order_id or only on sku. This creates order headers, product references, and true line facts. Third normal form is the second pass: within each resulting table, remove attributes that depend on a non-key attribute rather than the table key.

A useful phrasing is: 2NF asks whether the fact needs all of the key; 3NF asks whether the fact is being reached through another fact. In the example, order_date does not need all of order_id, sku, so it fails 2NF in the original table. customer_email is reached through customer_id after the order table exists, so it fails 3NF there. unit_price_at_order needs the order and the SKU together, so it remains a line fact.

The goal is not to maximize the number of tables. The goal is to make each stored fact live at the grain where it is true. Once the grain is explicit, constraints and joins can express the relationships: order lines reference orders and products, orders reference customers, and products reference categories. That model makes anomalies easier to spot because a change to a customer, product, or category has one natural place to occur.

takeaways: Second normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on only part of a composite key, such as order_date depending on order_id inside an order_id, sku table.
Third normal form removes non-key attributes that depend on another non-key attribute, such as customer_email depending on customer_id inside an orders table.
Do not move historical line facts, such as unit_price_at_order, into a product table unless the business rule really says SKU alone determines the value.
Dependency diagnostics can find counterexamples in sample data, but the final model still depends on declared business meaning.

title: Relational division for analytical questions
description: Use relational division to find entities that satisfy every requirement in a reference set, with a hypothetical retail example, counterexamples, and SQL patterns that avoid duplicate-counting mistakes.
lead: Many analytical questions are not asking whether an entity has any matching row. They are asking whether it has every required match. That is the relational division problem: given a set of entities, a set of requirements, and evidence that an entity satisfies a requirement, return the entities that satisfy the whole reference set.

sections.heading: The question relational division answers
paragraphs: Relational division is useful when the business question has the shape “which X has all required Y?” Common analytical examples include stores carrying every required product category, customers completing every onboarding step, accounts enabling every required security control, or suppliers certified for every required region.

The important part is the word every. A normal join answers “which entities have at least one matching requirement?” Aggregation can answer “how many requirements did each entity satisfy?” Relational division answers the stronger question: “for each required item, does a corresponding satisfaction row exist for this entity?”

In relational terms, imagine a relation S(entity_id, requirement_id) that records satisfied requirements and a relation R(requirement_id) that records the reference set. S divided by R returns the entity_id values whose set of satisfied requirements contains all requirement_id values in R. Extra satisfied requirements do not disqualify the entity; missing one required item does.

The rest of this article uses a small hypothetical retail dataset. The example is intentionally small enough to inspect by eye because the hard part is usually not syntax. The hard part is preserving the intended set semantics when the physical table contains duplicates, status rows, event grain, or extra categories.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Suppose a merchandising team defines a launch checklist for stores. A store qualifies for the launch only if it has active assortment coverage for every required category: backpack, notebook, and pencil.

The evidence table below is hypothetical. It is not customer or production data. The same shape would work for many other analytical requirements: replace store_id with account_id, category with onboarding_step, and active assortment with completed event.

Read the rows carefully before looking at the SQL. North qualifies because it has all three required categories. Central also qualifies even though pencil appears twice; duplicates should not hurt if the question is set membership. East is missing pencil. West has backpack only as inactive, so it is missing an active backpack. South is missing pencil but has a duplicate notebook row that can fool a row-count query. Outlet has three active rows but one is marker, which is not part of the required set.
bullets: Reference set: backpack, notebook, pencil.
Qualifying stores by inspection: north and central.
Non-qualifying counterexamples: east is incomplete, west fails the active-status rule, south has a duplicate instead of pencil, and outlet has an extra non-required category instead of backpack.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style SQL using common table expressions.
-- The example is self-contained and the expected result is derived from the rows shown here.
WITH required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES
    ('backpack'),
    ('notebook'),
    ('pencil')
),
store_category(store_id, category, status) AS (
  VALUES
    ('north',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('north',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('north',   'pencil',   'active'),
    ('north',   'marker',   'active'),

    ('east',    'backpack', 'active'),
    ('east',    'notebook', 'active'),

    ('west',    'backpack', 'inactive'),
    ('west',    'notebook', 'active'),
    ('west',    'pencil',   'active'),

    ('south',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('south',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('south',   'notebook', 'active'),

    ('central', 'backpack', 'active'),
    ('central', 'notebook', 'active'),
    ('central', 'pencil',   'active'),
    ('central', 'pencil',   'active'),

    ('outlet',  'notebook', 'active'),
    ('outlet',  'pencil',   'active'),
    ('outlet',  'marker',   'active')
)
SELECT *
FROM store_category;

sections.heading: The double NOT EXISTS pattern
paragraphs: The most direct SQL expression of relational division is a double anti-join: return stores for which there does not exist a required category that the store does not satisfy. It reads awkwardly at first, but it maps closely to the logic of “every.”

The inner NOT EXISTS asks: for this store and this required category, is there an active evidence row? The outer NOT EXISTS asks: is there any required category for which that evidence is missing? If no missing required category exists, the store qualifies.

This pattern is often the safest starting point because it does not depend on counting rows. Duplicates in the evidence table do not change the answer. Extra categories do not change the answer. Status filters can be placed exactly where the evidence is defined. The pattern still depends on the reference set having the intended meaning; if required_categories accidentally contains duplicate or invalid values, the model should be fixed rather than hidden in the query.

WITH required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('backpack'), ('notebook'), ('pencil')
),
store_category(store_id, category, status) AS (
  VALUES
    ('north',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('north',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('north',   'pencil',   'active'),
    ('north',   'marker',   'active'),
    ('east',    'backpack', 'active'),
    ('east',    'notebook', 'active'),
    ('west',    'backpack', 'inactive'),
    ('west',    'notebook', 'active'),
    ('west',    'pencil',   'active'),
    ('south',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('south',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('south',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('central', 'backpack', 'active'),
    ('central', 'notebook', 'active'),
    ('central', 'pencil',   'active'),
    ('central', 'pencil',   'active'),
    ('outlet',  'notebook', 'active'),
    ('outlet',  'pencil',   'active'),
    ('outlet',  'marker',   'active')
),
stores AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT store_id
  FROM store_category
)
SELECT s.store_id
FROM stores AS s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM required_categories AS r
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM store_category AS sc
    WHERE sc.store_id = s.store_id
      AND sc.category = r.category
      AND sc.status = 'active'
  )
)
ORDER BY s.store_id;

-- Expected result:
-- central
-- north

sections.heading: Why naive counting fails
paragraphs: A common shortcut is to count matching rows per store and compare the count with the number of required categories. That shortcut is only correct when the counted rows are already at the same grain as the requirement set: one row per store per required category after applying the relevant filters. If the table is at event grain or contains duplicates, row counts can lie.

In the hypothetical fixture, south has three active rows that match required categories: backpack, notebook, and notebook. A row-count query can incorrectly classify south as complete even though pencil is missing. Central has four active matching rows because pencil appears twice. A query that uses equality instead of greater-than-or-equal can incorrectly exclude central even though it satisfies all three categories.

Counting is not forbidden. The safer aggregation form is to count distinct required categories after joining to the reference set and applying the status rule. That expresses set coverage rather than physical row volume. Even then, it relies on the requirement set being unique at its own grain.

  VALUES ('backpack'), ('notebook'), ('pencil')
),

  VALUES
    ('north',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('north',   'notebook', 'active'),

sections.heading: Diagnose missing requirements, not just qualifying entities
paragraphs: A division query returns the winners. During development, it is often more useful to return the missing pairs. The diagnostic query below constructs the complete candidate grid of store by required category, then left joins the satisfied set. Rows with no match explain why a store failed.

This diagnostic also helps catch grain mistakes. If a store appears to be missing a category that users expect to be present, inspect whether the evidence was filtered out by status, whether category labels match the reference set exactly, and whether the source table is really at the grain implied by the query.

For production models, the reference set should usually be represented as a real table with a key such as program_id and category, not as a hard-coded VALUES list. PostgreSQL documentation describes constraints such as primary keys, unique constraints, and foreign keys; those are the database-level tools that keep the denominator and evidence relationships from drifting. The exact constraint design depends on the model, but the analytical requirement is simple: the denominator needs a trustworthy candidate key, and the evidence relation needs a well-defined grain.

codeExamples.code:
WITH required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('backpack'), ('notebook'), ('pencil')
),
store_category(store_id, category, status) AS (
  VALUES
    ('north',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('north',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('north',   'pencil',   'active'),
    ('north',   'marker',   'active'),
    ('east',    'backpack', 'active'),
    ('east',    'notebook', 'active'),
    ('west',    'backpack', 'inactive'),
    ('west',    'notebook', 'active'),
    ('west',    'pencil',   'active'),
    ('south',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('south',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('south',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('central', 'backpack', 'active'),
    ('central', 'notebook', 'active'),
    ('central', 'pencil',   'active'),
    ('central', 'pencil',   'active'),
    ('outlet',  'notebook', 'active'),
    ('outlet',  'pencil',   'active'),
    ('outlet',  'marker',   'active')
),
stores AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT store_id
  FROM store_category
),
satisfied AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT store_id, category
  FROM store_category
  WHERE status = 'active'
)
SELECT s.store_id, r.category AS missing_category
FROM stores AS s
CROSS JOIN required_categories AS r
LEFT JOIN satisfied AS sat
  ON sat.store_id = s.store_id
 AND sat.category = r.category
WHERE sat.store_id IS NULL
ORDER BY s.store_id, r.category;

-- Expected result:
-- east    pencil
-- outlet  backpack
-- south   pencil
-- west    backpack

sections.heading: Modeling rules for “every” questions
paragraphs: Relational division is a query pattern, but the quality of the answer is mostly determined before the query runs. The model has to make the denominator explicit, define what counts as satisfaction, and preserve the grain of both sides.

First, name the reference set. “Every required category” should point to a table or derived relation that can be inspected. If the requirement changes by program, region, customer tier, or date, those attributes belong in the denominator’s key. A single unqualified list of categories is only correct when the requirement is truly global.

Second, derive a satisfaction relation at the same grain as the denominator before dividing. In the example, that relation is distinct store_id and category where status is active. If the source is an order-event table, derive distinct customer_id and required_step after filtering to completed events. If the source is a slowly changing table, decide which version is in force before asking the division question.

Third, decide what an empty reference set means. In formal logic, every entity satisfies every requirement in an empty set because there is no missing requirement. That is called vacuous truth. Some analytical use cases accept that result; many business reports do not. If an empty denominator should produce no qualifying entities, add an explicit EXISTS check for the reference set.

Finally, treat NULLs deliberately. A NULL category in the evidence table is not the same as a known required category. A NULL in the denominator usually means the reference set is not well-defined. The cleaner fix is to prevent unknown requirement identifiers from entering the denominator, not to rely on a division query to guess the intended meaning.
bullets: Make the denominator inspectable and keyed at the requirement grain.
Define satisfaction as a relation, not as an accidental count of physical rows.
Use double NOT EXISTS when you want the clearest expression of “no missing requirement.”
Use COUNT(DISTINCT requirement) only after aligning filters and grain.
Add an explicit non-empty-denominator rule when vacuous truth is not acceptable.

codeExamples.code:
-- Optional guard when an empty reference set should return no stores.
-- This keeps the double NOT EXISTS logic but requires at least one required category.
WITH required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('backpack'), ('notebook'), ('pencil')
),
store_category(store_id, category, status) AS (
  VALUES
    ('north',   'backpack', 'active'),
    ('north',   'notebook', 'active'),
    ('north',   'pencil',   'active')
),
stores AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT store_id
  FROM store_category
)
SELECT s.store_id
FROM stores AS s
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM required_categories)
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM required_categories AS r
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM store_category AS sc
      WHERE sc.store_id = s.store_id
        AND sc.category = r.category
        AND sc.status = 'active'
    )
  );

takeaways: Relational division answers “which entities satisfy every requirement in this reference set?” rather than “which entities have any matching row?”
The double NOT EXISTS pattern is a clear SQL expression of “there is no required item missing for this entity.”
Naive row counts fail when the evidence table has duplicates, extra categories, event grain, or status rows; count distinct requirements only after aligning grain and filters.
A diagnostic missing-requirements query is often the fastest way to validate the denominator, filters, and expected result.
Decide explicitly how to handle empty reference sets and NULL requirement values before publishing the metric.

title: Floating-point error in financial analytics
description: A practical guide to demonstrating representation error in repeated decimal arithmetic, with explicit calculation rules and a diagnostic query for financial analytics data.
lead: Financial analytics often starts with decimal amounts: prices, discounts, fees, refunds, balances, and adjustments. The trap is that many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly by binary floating-point types. The error is usually tiny, but repeated arithmetic can make it visible in reconciliations, equality checks, and threshold logic. This guide shows how to demonstrate the error without turning the topic into tax or accounting advice.

sections.heading: Why decimal amounts become inexact
paragraphs: A decimal amount such as 0.10 looks simple because humans write it in base 10. Binary floating-point systems store numbers in base 2. A fraction has a terminating representation in base 2 only when its reduced denominator is a power of 2. The fraction 1/10 does not meet that rule because its denominator includes a factor of 5. Therefore, 0.10 cannot be stored exactly as a finite binary fraction.

This is a representation problem before it is an aggregation problem. If the stored value is already slightly above or below the intended decimal amount, summing that stored value many times repeats the small difference. Arithmetic rounding during the aggregation can add more differences, and the order of operations can affect the final displayed result.

PostgreSQL’s documentation makes the distinction directly: numeric is an exact numeric type, while floating-point types are inexact. The exact type is the natural default for stored financial amounts when decimal correctness matters. This article does not choose a precision and scale for a production schema; it focuses only on demonstrating why repeated decimal arithmetic can diverge when represented as floating point.
bullets: A decimal fraction terminates in binary only when the denominator, after reducing the fraction, has no prime factors except 2.
0.50 is exactly representable in binary because 1/2 has denominator 2.
0.25 is exactly representable in binary because 1/4 has denominator 4.
0.10 is not exactly representable in binary because 1/10 has denominator 10, which includes 5.
The error may be far smaller than one cent, but it can still break exact comparisons or produce confusing reconciliation deltas.

sections.heading: A paper counterexample with explicit rules
paragraphs: A coarse paper model makes the mechanism visible without relying on any database engine or programming language. This is not a claim about the size of error in a real binary64 implementation. It is a deliberately exaggerated model that uses binary-sized steps so the representation error can be calculated by hand.

Assume a hypothetical retail promotion file contains ten customer-event rows. Each row is intended to carry a 0.10 dollar loyalty credit. Now assume the storage model can represent only sixteenths of a dollar: 0/16, 1/16, 2/16, and so on. This is a binary grid because the denominator is a power of 2. Use this rule: when a decimal amount enters the system, convert it to the nearest sixteenth of a dollar, and then aggregate the represented values exactly.

Under that rule, 0.10 dollars equals 1.6/16 dollars. The nearest representable value is 2/16, which is 0.125 dollars. The representation error per row is 0.125 minus 0.10, or 0.025 dollars. Across ten rows, the intended sum is 10 times 0.10, which is 1.00 dollar. The represented sum is 10 times 0.125, which is 1.25 dollars. The aggregate error is 0.25 dollars.

The grid is intentionally crude, but the lesson is the same for real binary floating-point systems: a decimal amount is first mapped to a nearby representable binary value. Repetition turns a per-row representation difference into an aggregate difference. Real systems use much finer grids, so the error for ordinary cent values is normally much smaller than this paper model. The counterexample is useful because it separates the source of error from formatting, display, and accounting policy.
bullets: Hypothetical input: 10 retail credit events at 0.10 dollars each.
Representation rule: store only nearest sixteenth-dollar values.
Per-row conversion: 0.10 dollars becomes 0.125 dollars.
Intended aggregate: 10 × 0.10 = 1.00 dollars.
Represented aggregate: 10 × 0.125 = 1.25 dollars.
Demonstrated error: 1.25 − 1.00 = 0.25 dollars.

sections.heading: What changes in real floating point
paragraphs: Real binary floating-point formats are not as coarse as the paper model. For example, the commonly used binary64 format has enough precision that the stored value nearest to 0.10 dollars is very close to 0.10. One exact decimal rendering of the nearest binary64 value for 0.10 is 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625. The representation error is about 0.000000000000000005551 dollars per value.

If one million hypothetical events each intend to add 0.10 dollars, the representation component alone is approximately one million times that per-value error: 0.0000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 dollars. That is much less than a cent. The point is not that every floating-point sum of cents will be materially wrong. The point is that the result is not exactly the same mathematical object as a decimal sum.

Sequential floating-point addition can introduce additional rounding at each step. Parallel aggregation can also combine partial sums in different orders. Those effects mean a real engine’s final floating sum is not always equal to the simple per-row representation error multiplied by row count. The paper model answers the question, “Where did inexactness enter?” A database diagnostic answers the separate question, “How large is the observed difference in this calculation?”

For financial analytics, the dangerous assumption is exact equality. If a reconciliation check expects a floating result to equal a decimal result bit-for-bit, it can fail for reasons unrelated to the business event being measured. If a threshold rule compares a value near a boundary, a tiny representation difference can push a row to the other side of the comparison. The safer habit is to store and aggregate financial amounts with exact decimal or integer minor-unit representations, then use floating point only for calculations where approximate numeric behavior is acceptable.

sections.heading: An illustrative PostgreSQL diagnostic
paragraphs: The following query is illustrative PostgreSQL 18 SQL. It is not presented as executed evidence. It shows the shape of a diagnostic that compares a repeated decimal amount parsed as numeric with the same amount parsed as double precision. PostgreSQL’s numeric documentation describes numeric as an exact type, and its aggregate documentation describes aggregate functions such as sum. The useful diagnostic is the difference between an exact decimal aggregate and an approximate floating aggregate at the same grain.

The dataset is hypothetical. It represents one million customer credit events, each carrying the text amount 0.10. Keeping the input as text in the fixture makes the conversion point explicit: the same source token is cast once to numeric and once to double precision. In an actual pipeline, the diagnostic should run at the business grain that matters, such as invoice, order, refund batch, merchant day, or ledger posting group.

The reported difference should be interpreted with scale. A difference of one ten-billionth of a dollar may be harmless for a dashboard total but still harmful if the downstream logic requires exact equality. NIST’s discussion of measures of scale is a reminder that magnitude matters: always report the absolute difference, and when useful, also report it relative to the size of the aggregate.
bullets: Use the original source token when possible so the diagnostic compares conversion choices rather than two already-transformed columns.
Group by the reconciliation grain, not only by the whole table.
Report row count, exact decimal sum, floating sum rendered for inspection, absolute difference, and difference in cents.
Do not use this diagnostic as tax, revenue-recognition, or accounting policy. It is a numeric representation check.

codeExamples.code:
WITH hypothetical_events AS (
    SELECT
        gs AS event_id,
        '0.10'::text AS amount_text
    FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) AS gs
)
SELECT
    count(*) AS event_count,
    sum(amount_text::numeric) AS numeric_sum,
    sum(amount_text::double precision)::numeric AS float_sum_rendered_as_numeric,
    sum(amount_text::double precision)::numeric - sum(amount_text::numeric) AS difference_dollars,
    100 * (sum(amount_text::double precision)::numeric - sum(amount_text::numeric)) AS difference_cents
FROM hypothetical_events;

sections.heading: Calculation rules for practitioners
paragraphs: A durable way to reason about this problem is to separate representation, aggregation, and presentation. Representation is the type used to store each value. Aggregation is the arithmetic used to combine many values. Presentation is the final formatting shown to people. Floating-point confusion often appears when these stages are mixed together, such as formatting a float to two decimals and assuming the underlying value is now a two-decimal financial amount.

For a representation-error demonstration, use exact rules and keep the fixture small enough to understand. Start with decimal source tokens. Define the intended decimal value. Define the approximate representation rule, whether it is the hand-calculated sixteenth-dollar model or a real database cast to a floating type. Aggregate both paths. Compare the two results before any final display rounding.

For production modeling, the common rule is simple: do not store money-like facts as approximate floating point when exact decimal behavior is required. Use an exact decimal type or an integer minor unit such as cents, depending on the modeling requirements. Floating point remains appropriate for many analytical measures, including ratios, statistical features, scientific measurements, and approximate scores. The issue is not that floating point is bad; the issue is using an approximate representation where the business meaning requires exact decimal arithmetic.
bullets: Rule 1: identify the source decimal token, such as 0.10.
Rule 2: state the intended exact value, such as 1/10 dollar.
Rule 3: state the representation rule, such as nearest binary value or nearest sixteenth in a paper model.
Rule 4: aggregate represented values and exact values separately.
Rule 5: compare before presentation rounding so display formatting does not hide the numeric behavior.
Rule 6: decide whether the observed difference matters for the downstream use case: reconciliation, equality, thresholding, ranking, or display only.

sections.heading: Common counterexamples and traps
paragraphs: A frequent counterargument is that floating-point error is too small to matter for ordinary financial dashboards. Sometimes that is true. If the dashboard only shows rounded, high-level totals and no downstream process depends on exact equality, the observed error may be operationally irrelevant. But that does not make the representation exact. The right conclusion is conditional: approximate arithmetic may be acceptable for a specific analytical use, but it should not be mistaken for exact decimal arithmetic.

Another trap is checking only the final formatted output. A report that displays 1000.00 after formatting may still have used an inexact intermediate value. Formatting is not the same as storage, and it is not the same as aggregation. If another job consumes the unformatted value, joins on it, compares it to a decimal total, or uses it near a threshold, the hidden difference can reappear.

A third trap is assuming that one successful sample proves safety. Floating-point aggregation can be sensitive to values, row counts, grouping, and order of operations. A useful diagnostic should include cases with repeated small decimals, mixed signs such as charges and refunds, large and small values in the same group, and values near decision thresholds. The goal is not to prove that every result is wrong. The goal is to find whether the pipeline is relying on exactness that the representation does not provide.
bullets: Do not test only values such as 0.50 and 0.25; they are exactly representable in binary and can hide the problem.
Do include values such as 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 because their decimal fractions are not generally exact in binary.
Do not treat two-decimal display as evidence of two-decimal storage.
Do not compare approximate floating aggregates with exact decimal aggregates using equality unless the purpose is to detect this exact failure mode.

takeaways: Floating-point error in financial analytics starts with representation: many decimal fractions, including 0.10, do not have finite binary representations.
Repeated arithmetic can make a tiny per-value representation difference visible, especially in equality checks, reconciliation diagnostics, and threshold logic.
A good demonstration separates exact decimal aggregation from approximate floating aggregation and compares them before presentation rounding.
For money-like stored facts that require exact decimal behavior, prefer exact decimal or integer minor-unit representations over approximate floating-point types.

title: Fixed-point decimal precision and scale
description: A practical guide to choosing decimal precision and scale for stored values, products, and aggregates without under-sizing intermediate calculations.
lead: Choosing DECIMAL or NUMERIC columns is not just a storage decision. It is a capacity decision for the largest value you will store, the smallest unit you must preserve, and the widest intermediate result your transformations can produce. The common mistake is sizing the final column but forgetting that multiplication and aggregation need more digits than any single input row.

sections.heading: The capacity question behind precision and scale
paragraphs: Fixed-point decimal types are usually written as DECIMAL(p, s) or NUMERIC(p, s). PostgreSQL documentation describes precision as the total number of significant digits and scale as the number of digits to the right of the decimal point. That definition is compact, but the modeling question is more practical: how many digits are available before the decimal point, and how many are reserved after it?

For a decimal value with precision p and scale s, the integer-side capacity is p minus s digits. DECIMAL(12, 2) has ten digits to the left of the decimal point and two to the right. Its largest positive value is 9,999,999,999.99. More generally, if i is the number of integer digits and s is the scale, the maximum absolute value below the next power of ten is 10^i minus 10^-s.

That means a column definition answers two different questions. The scale answers the unit question: cents, basis points, kilograms to three decimals, seconds to six decimals, and so on. The integer digits answer the capacity question: how large can the value become before it no longer fits? Practitioners get into trouble when they pick scale from the business unit but pick precision by habit.

This article is about numeric representation and aggregation capacity. It is not tax, accounting, or revenue-recognition advice. If the business rule says a value must be rounded at a specific stage, model that rule separately. The sizing problem here is narrower: given the values you intend to preserve and the calculations you intend to run, choose decimal capacity that does not surprise you.

sections.heading: Rules for sizing stored decimal values
paragraphs: Start with stored values, not derived values. For each decimal column, write down the unit, the sign policy, the maximum absolute value you expect to admit, and the number of fractional digits that must be preserved. Then translate that into integer digits plus scale.

The integer digit count is the number of digits needed to represent the largest allowed absolute value before the decimal point. If the largest allowed unit price is 99,999.99, it needs five integer digits and two fractional digits, so DECIMAL(7, 2) is the minimum shape. If the largest allowed quantity is 9,999 whole units, it needs DECIMAL(4, 0).

Minimum shape is rarely the operational shape. A minimum that exactly matches today’s largest allowed value leaves no room for policy changes, upstream mistakes that should be quarantined rather than truncated, or longer-lived historical tables. A better design records the business maximum separately from the physical capacity. For example, a data contract might reject unit prices above 99,999.99 while the warehouse column is still sized with a little extra headroom.
Use this checklist before choosing p and s:
bullets: Choose scale from the smallest unit you must preserve, not from how values are displayed. A value displayed as dollars may still need cents or sub-cent precision internally.
Choose integer digits from the largest admitted absolute value, including sign. The sign itself is not a digit, but negative values need the same magnitude capacity as positive values.
Separate business validation from physical capacity. The column can be wider than the allowed business range.

Avoid using statistical scale terms as substitutes for decimal scale. In statistics, measures of scale describe spread or dispersion; in DECIMAL(p, s), scale is a digit count to the right of the decimal point.
Document whether zeros after the decimal point are meaningful. DECIMAL(10, 4) and DECIMAL(10, 2) can both store 12.34, but they communicate different precision expectations.

sections.heading: Rules for products, sums, and averages
paragraphs: The stored columns are only the first part of the sizing problem. Transformations often create intermediate values that need more capacity than any input column. A safe mental model is to carry integer digits and fractional digits through the calculation explicitly.

For addition and subtraction, align scales. The result scale must be at least the maximum input scale if you want to preserve the inputs without rounding. The integer-side capacity must fit the largest possible sum of magnitudes, not just the largest row. If a value has i integer digits and you may sum up to n nonnegative rows, budget i plus ceiling(log10(n)) integer digits. This is a worst-case capacity rule. It assumes every row can be near its maximum at the same time.

For multiplication, add scales and add integer digit capacities. If DECIMAL(7, 2) can hold values up to 99,999.99 and DECIMAL(4, 0) can hold values up to 9,999, the exact product needs two fractional digits and up to nine integer digits. The resulting shape is DECIMAL(11, 2): nine integer digits plus two fractional digits. The maximum product under those input bounds is 999,899,900.01, which confirms the nine integer digits.

Division is not as tidy because terminating and repeating decimals depend on the divisor. Capacity planning for division should be explicit: decide the output scale required by the business meaning, calculate with enough guard digits if the engine supports it, then round or cast once at the chosen boundary. Do not let an accidental default scale become the business rule.

Averages are also a two-stage problem. The average value may fit in the same integer capacity as the inputs, but the intermediate sum may not. If you average two billion values of DECIMAL(12, 2), the final average might fit in DECIMAL(12, 2), while the sum can require far more integer digits. Size the sum first, then the final average.
bullets: Addition or subtraction: result scale is max(s1, s2, ...); integer capacity must account for the largest possible combined magnitude.
Sum of n nonnegative values: integer digits needed are input integer digits plus ceiling(log10(n)).
Multiplication: result scale is s1 plus s2; integer digits needed are i1 plus i2.
Average: size the intermediate sum using the sum rule, then choose the final average scale intentionally.
Division: choose an output scale as a modeling decision because exact decimal expansion is not guaranteed.

sections.heading: Worked example: hypothetical retail line items
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order dataset. Each line item has a unit price, a quantity, and a derived line amount. The values are deliberately simple so the capacity math is visible.

Assumptions: unit_price is stored as DECIMAL(7, 2), allowing values up to 99,999.99. quantity is stored as DECIMAL(4, 0), allowing values up to 9,999. line_amount is computed as quantity multiplied by unit_price. A store-day aggregate may include up to 50,000 line items.

First calculate the product. unit_price has five integer digits and two fractional digits. quantity has four integer digits and zero fractional digits. The product therefore needs nine integer digits and two fractional digits, so line_amount needs DECIMAL(11, 2) if it must preserve the exact product of the admitted inputs. The maximum product is 9,999 multiplied by 99,999.99, which equals 999,899,900.01.

Now calculate the store-day sum. line_amount has nine integer digits and two fractional digits. The aggregate may include 50,000 lines. ceiling(log10(50,000)) is 5 because 50,000 is between 10,000 and 100,000. The worst-case sum needs 9 plus 5, or 14 integer digits, and still needs two fractional digits. A store-day sales amount therefore needs DECIMAL(16, 2) under these assumptions.

This is larger than many teams would choose by looking only at sample data. If yesterday’s maximum line amount was 2,000.00, DECIMAL(9, 2) might appear safe. But the column definitions admit a much larger value. Capacity should be based on admitted bounds and aggregation grain, not only on observed history.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL shape for the hypothetical model.
-- The arithmetic is shown for capacity planning; adapt syntax and generated-column behavior to your database engine.

CREATE TABLE retail_order_line_hypothetical (
    order_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
    line_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
    store_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
    order_date      DATE NOT NULL,
    unit_price      DECIMAL(7, 2) NOT NULL,
    quantity        DECIMAL(4, 0) NOT NULL,
    line_amount     DECIMAL(11, 2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_id)
);

-- Capacity rule used for the aggregate:
-- line_amount: 9 integer digits, 2 fractional digits
-- up to 50,000 rows per store-day: ceiling(log10(50000)) = 5
-- store-day sum: 14 integer digits, 2 fractional digits => DECIMAL(16, 2)

CREATE TABLE retail_store_day_sales_hypothetical (
    store_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
    order_date      DATE NOT NULL,
    line_count      INTEGER NOT NULL,
    sales_amount    DECIMAL(16, 2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (store_id, order_date)
);

sections.heading: Counterexample: the column fits, but the aggregate does not
paragraphs: A common counterexample is a transaction table where each row amount is correctly sized, but the reporting table is not. Suppose transaction_amount is DECIMAL(12, 2). That gives ten integer digits and two fractional digits, so a single transaction can be as large as 9,999,999,999.99.

Now suppose a monthly customer, product, or merchant aggregate can include up to 2,000,000,000 rows. The sum needs ten input integer digits plus ceiling(log10(2,000,000,000)) more digits. Because 2,000,000,000 has ten digits, the aggregate can require twenty integer digits. Preserving cents means two fractional digits, so the safe aggregate shape is DECIMAL(22, 2).

If the aggregate table is defined as DECIMAL(12, 2) because the source column is DECIMAL(12, 2), the design has confused row capacity with aggregate capacity. Even DECIMAL(18, 2) is not enough under the stated worst-case assumptions; it provides only sixteen integer digits. The final report may rarely approach this bound, but the capacity decision should be tied to an explicit row-count bound or an explicit decision to reject, segment, or separately handle larger groups.

This does not mean every aggregate must be sized for absurd theoretical maxima. It means the assumption should be visible. If the real business rule says an aggregate partition cannot exceed 5,000,000 rows, use that number. If no such rule exists, the model is relying on hope rather than capacity planning.

sections.heading: A diagnostic before changing decimal definitions
paragraphs: Before tightening, widening, or standardizing decimal definitions, inventory both stored values and calculation paths. The useful output is not just a list of current maximums. It is a list of admitted maximums, observed maximums, aggregation grains, and derived-field formulas.

Observed profiling still matters. It can reveal that source data already exceeds the business assumption, or that a supposedly whole-number field contains fractional values. But observed data cannot prove future capacity unless the upstream contract enforces the same bound. Treat profiling as evidence about current data quality, not as the only sizing input.

For duration and lag facts, the same rules apply. Dimensional models often store elapsed time as a fact. If a duration is stored in seconds with three fractional digits, its scale is three; if it is later summed across many events, the aggregate duration needs additional integer digits. The fact that the measure is time rather than money does not change the capacity arithmetic.
bullets: For every stored decimal, record integer digits, scale, allowed sign, and business maximum.
For every derived decimal, write the formula and compute the required intermediate shape before choosing the stored output shape.
For every aggregate, record the maximum group size or partition size used in the capacity calculation.
For every cast, identify whether it is preserving capacity, intentionally rounding, or accidentally narrowing.
For every dashboard or downstream table, check whether it stores row-level capacity or aggregate-level capacity.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative profiling query for a hypothetical decimal column.
-- This finds observed magnitudes; it does not replace business capacity rules.

SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS row_count,
    MAX(ABS(transaction_amount)) AS observed_max_abs_amount,
    SUM(CASE WHEN transaction_amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS negative_row_count
FROM fact_transaction_hypothetical;

-- Pair observed profiling with explicit modeling notes such as:
-- source shape: DECIMAL(12, 2)
-- integer digits: 10
-- aggregate grain: merchant-month
-- maximum rows per merchant-month used for sizing: 2,000,000,000
-- required sum shape: DECIMAL(22, 2)

sections.heading: A practical decision framework
paragraphs: A useful decimal definition can be explained without referring to whatever happened to fit in a sample file. The explanation should connect the business unit, the admitted range, and the largest planned calculation.

Use the following process. First, pick scale from the smallest unit that must survive storage. Second, choose the admitted maximum absolute value and translate it into integer digits. Third, calculate derived products, sums, and averages using explicit propagation rules. Fourth, decide where rounding or narrowing is intentional. Fifth, add physical headroom if the table is long-lived or if upstream limits are enforced outside the database.

The tradeoff is that wider decimals can be less convenient and may have storage or execution costs depending on the database engine. But narrowing too early creates a correctness risk that is harder to diagnose later. In data engineering work, the safer default is to preserve capacity through raw and intermediate layers, then narrow only at a clearly named presentation, export, or contract boundary.

The result should be a short capacity note attached to the model: DECIMAL(16, 2) because line_amount has nine integer digits, the store-day group can contain up to 50,000 lines, and the sum therefore needs fourteen integer digits plus cents. That note is more useful than a bare type declaration because it lets the next engineer challenge the assumptions instead of reverse-engineering them.

takeaways: Precision is total digit capacity; scale is the number of digits to the right of the decimal point. Integer-side capacity is precision minus scale.
Stored row values, derived products, and aggregate sums often require different decimal shapes. Do not reuse the source column type for every downstream result by default.
For multiplication, add integer digit capacities and add scales. For summing up to n nonnegative rows, add ceiling(log10(n)) integer digits to the input integer capacity.
Observed maximums are useful diagnostics, but capacity should be based on admitted bounds, formulas, and aggregation grain.
Document the assumptions behind each decimal definition so future changes can update the bound rather than guess why the type was chosen.

title: Rounding at ingestion versus presentation
description: A practical guide to showing how the stage where you round numeric values can change reconciled aggregate totals, with a hypothetical retail example and diagnostic SQL.
lead: Rounding is not just a display choice when it happens before aggregation. If a pipeline rounds each row at ingestion and then sums those rounded rows, it can produce a different reconciled total than a pipeline that sums the unrounded values and rounds only the displayed result. The difference is usually small per row, but it becomes visible when teams compare dashboards, aggregate fact tables, extracts, and source-system totals.

sections.heading: The problem: rounding changes the grain of the fact
paragraphs: The question is not whether rounded numbers are easier to read. They are. The question is whether the rounded value becomes the stored fact used for later aggregation. Once a pipeline replaces 1.005 with 1.01, the original 0.005 has been absorbed into the row. Summing many such rows is no longer the same calculation as summing the original values.

This matters in data modeling because most analytic totals are aggregates over a chosen grain: order line, shipment, subscription day, customer event, account month, or another atomic unit. Aggregate functions such as SUM add the input values they are given. They do not know whether those inputs are raw measurements, already-rounded presentation values, or authoritative settled cents.

This article stays within numeric representation and aggregation. It is not tax, accounting, or revenue-recognition advice. In some domains, the rounded amount at a specific grain is the authoritative business fact. In other domains, early rounding is only a convenience that accidentally becomes logic.

sections.heading: Two explicit calculation rules
paragraphs: Use explicit rules before comparing totals. Ambiguous phrases like “round the amount” are the source of many reconciliation arguments. The following rules are deliberately narrow and use non-negative hypothetical retail order-line amounts. The rounding rule is half up to two decimal places for positive values: multiply by 100, add 0.5, take the floor, and divide by 100.
Rule A is ingestion rounding. Compute or receive a raw line amount, round each line to cents at ingestion, store that rounded line amount, and sum stored line amounts for reports.

Rule B is presentation rounding. Store the raw decimal line amount at enough precision for the metric, sum the raw line amounts at the reporting grain, and round only the final displayed aggregate to cents.

Those rules answer different business questions. Rule A asks, “What is the total of the rounded line facts?” Rule B asks, “What is the rounded total of the unrounded line facts?” The two questions sound similar, but they are not algebraically equivalent. In general, SUM(ROUND(x, 2)) does not equal ROUND(SUM(x), 2).
bullets: Rule A: total_ingestion_rounded = SUM(round_each_line_to_cents(raw_line_amount)).
Rule B: total_presentation_rounded = round_to_cents(SUM(raw_line_amount)).
Diagnostic residual: rounding_stage_difference = total_ingestion_rounded - total_presentation_rounded.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail counterexample
paragraphs: Consider this hypothetical retail-order fixture. The raw amount might come from a proportional promotion, unit conversion, or another upstream calculation that produces more than two decimal places. The example uses only positive values so the half-up formula is unambiguous.

There are eight order lines: two at 1.005, two at 2.335, two at 3.335, and two at 4.445. Under Rule A, each line is rounded first. The rounded line amounts are 1.01, 1.01, 2.34, 2.34, 3.34, 3.34, 4.45, and 4.45. Their sum is 22.28.
Under Rule B, the raw values are summed first: 1.005 + 1.005 + 2.335 + 2.335 + 3.335 + 3.335 + 4.445 + 4.445 = 22.240. Rounded once for presentation, the total is 22.24.

The reconciled totals differ by 0.04. No row is “wrong” under its own rule. The mismatch appears because the two pipelines answer different questions. A dashboard built from ingestion-rounded facts will reconcile to 22.28. A dashboard built from raw facts and presentation rounding will reconcile to 22.24. If the metric owner never specifies the stage, both teams can claim they rounded to cents and still disagree.
bullets: Ingestion-rounded total: 22.28.
Presentation-rounded total: 22.24.
Difference: 0.04, caused only by the rounding stage in this hypothetical fixture.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style diagnostic for non-negative hypothetical amounts.
-- The half-up expression is written explicitly instead of relying on a
-- database-specific tie-breaking rule for ROUND.
WITH line_items(line_id, raw_amount) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 1.005::numeric),
    (2, 1.005::numeric),
    (3, 2.335::numeric),
    (4, 2.335::numeric),
    (5, 3.335::numeric),
    (6, 3.335::numeric),
    (7, 4.445::numeric),
    (8, 4.445::numeric)
), calculated AS (
  SELECT
    line_id,
    raw_amount,
    floor(raw_amount * 100 + 0.5) / 100 AS line_amount_rounded_half_up
  FROM line_items
)
SELECT
  sum(line_amount_rounded_half_up) AS ingestion_rounded_total,
  floor(sum(raw_amount) * 100 + 0.5) / 100 AS presentation_rounded_total,
  sum(line_amount_rounded_half_up)
    - floor(sum(raw_amount) * 100 + 0.5) / 100 AS rounding_stage_difference
FROM calculated;

sections.heading: Why aggregate tables amplify the choice
paragraphs: Aggregate fact tables and cubes are intentionally pre-summarized versions of lower-grain facts. They can improve usability and query performance, but they also freeze modeling choices. If an aggregate table is built from rounded line facts, every downstream report inherits ingestion rounding. If it is built from raw line facts and rounds only final measures, it inherits presentation rounding.

The important design point is lineage of the measure, not the existence of an aggregate table. A daily sales aggregate with a column named sales_amount could mean “sum of stored line cents” or “rounded sum of precise line calculations.” Those are different metrics even when they share a label.

A safe aggregate design keeps the rule visible in the transformation, metric definition, and column naming. For example, line_amount_cents_authoritative suggests a source-provided settled cent amount. line_amount_raw_decimal suggests an intermediate calculation that should not be shown directly as currency. daily_sales_amount_display suggests a final presentation measure. The names do not replace documentation, but they make accidental reuse less likely.
bullets: Build aggregate fact tables from the same numeric rule that the metric definition requires.
Do not mix rounded line facts and raw line facts in one measure without an explicit reconciliation column.
Treat a change in rounding stage as a metric definition change, not a formatting cleanup.

sections.heading: A diagnostic for existing pipelines
paragraphs: For an existing model, the fastest useful diagnostic is to calculate both totals side by side at the reconciliation grain. Use the grain at which humans compare numbers: invoice, order, store-day, customer-month, campaign, or accounting period. A global residual over a year can hide groups where positive and negative differences cancel.

The diagnostic below assumes a table with one row per hypothetical order line and a raw decimal amount. It groups by order_date so the residual can be inspected by day. The same pattern can be applied by order_id, store_id, customer_id, or metric version.

A nonzero residual is not automatically a bug. It is evidence that the rounding stage matters for that metric. The next step is to decide which total is supposed to reconcile to the authoritative source. If the source system issues settled line amounts in cents, sum those authoritative cents. If the source system emits high-precision calculated measurements for analytics, preserve the higher precision and round at the metric’s presentation boundary.
bullets: Run the comparison at the same grain used for reconciliation.
Count affected groups, not only the grand total residual.
Investigate the sign and distribution of residuals; cancellation can hide material local differences.
Record the chosen rule in the metric contract or semantic model.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostic pattern. Replace table and column names with
-- the model being reconciled. Assumes non-negative amounts and explicit
-- half-up rounding to cents.
SELECT
  order_date,
  count(*) AS line_count,
  sum(floor(raw_line_amount * 100 + 0.5) / 100) AS sum_of_rounded_lines,
  floor(sum(raw_line_amount) * 100 + 0.5) / 100 AS rounded_sum_of_raw_lines,
  sum(floor(raw_line_amount * 100 + 0.5) / 100)
    - floor(sum(raw_line_amount) * 100 + 0.5) / 100 AS rounding_stage_residual
FROM hypothetical_order_lines
GROUP BY order_date
HAVING sum(floor(raw_line_amount * 100 + 0.5) / 100)
    <> floor(sum(raw_line_amount) * 100 + 0.5) / 100
ORDER BY abs(
  sum(floor(raw_line_amount * 100 + 0.5) / 100)
    - floor(sum(raw_line_amount) * 100 + 0.5) / 100
) DESC;

sections.heading: A practical decision framework
paragraphs: Choose ingestion rounding when the rounded value is the fact. Examples include source-provided settled amounts, contractual units that are defined at a fixed minor unit, or records where downstream systems must reproduce the exact line-level amount shown to a customer. In those cases, storing additional calculated precision may be useful for audit or explanation, but it should not replace the authoritative amount used for reconciliation.

Choose presentation rounding when the raw value is the fact and cents are only a display format. Examples include rates, ratios, allocations before final distribution, sensor-derived costs, and analytic estimates. In those cases, early rounding throws away information and can bias aggregates when many rows have fractional remainders in the same direction.

For many pipelines, the right answer is to store both values with different meanings: an authoritative rounded amount if one exists, and a raw calculation amount for analytic recomputation. The key is to avoid letting a presentation-formatted value masquerade as the only reusable fact.

Also define how negative numbers and ties are handled. This article used non-negative values and an explicit half-up formula to keep the counterexample focused. Real datasets may include refunds, reversals, credits, and negative adjustments. The rounding rule should state whether ties move away from zero, toward zero, to even, or according to a platform-specific function. Do not assume that two systems use the same tie-breaking rule just because both display two decimal places.
bullets: If the source amount is authoritative at cents, aggregate that amount.
If the source amount is a high-precision analytic value, preserve it and round at presentation.
If both are needed, store both with names that expose their meaning.
Specify scale, rounding stage, and tie-breaking rule in the metric definition.

sections.heading: What to document in the metric definition
paragraphs: A metric definition should make the rounding stage testable. A reviewer should be able to look at a transformation and tell whether it implements the intended rule. The following fields are enough for most data engineering teams: input measure, storage precision, authoritative grain, aggregation rule, rounding stage, display scale, tie-breaking rule, and reconciliation target.

For the hypothetical example, a Rule A metric could be documented as: sales_amount is the sum of order-line amounts rounded to cents at ingestion using half-up rounding; it reconciles to the stored line amount extract. A Rule B metric could be documented as: sales_amount is the raw decimal sum of order-line calculations, rounded to cents only for display using half-up rounding; it reconciles to the high-precision calculation source.

That documentation prevents a common failure mode: one team compares a BI dashboard to an aggregate table while another compares an export to raw line items. Both are using SUM, but they are summing different facts. Clear rounding-stage rules turn that disagreement into a small, reproducible calculation instead of a vague trust issue.
bullets: Name the input value being summed.
State whether rounding occurs before or after aggregation.
State the rounding mode for ties and negative values.
State the reconciliation target the metric is expected to match.

takeaways: Rounding before aggregation and rounding after aggregation are different calculations; SUM(rounded rows) can differ from ROUND(SUM(raw rows)).
A nonzero rounding-stage residual is not automatically a defect. It shows that the metric definition must identify the authoritative rounding stage.
Aggregate tables should preserve the same rounding rule as the metric they serve, because pre-summarization freezes the chosen interpretation.
Document the input measure, aggregation rule, rounding stage, display scale, tie-breaking rule, and reconciliation target so totals can be reproduced.
